title: U.S. rushes extra fighter jets to Baltic skies as Russia flexes its military muscle!
text: The United States is not taking any chances. It has sent a reinforced detachment of fighter planes to police the skies over NATO members Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia during a major Russian military exercise in the Baltic region next month. The Zapad war games, running from Sept. 14 to 20 in Belarus, western Russia and Russia's exclave of Kaliningrad, have rattled the region. Russia insists the large-scale exercise will rehearse a purely defensive scenario and will not be a springboard for invasion. But who is reassured? Seven U.S. F-15C fighters roared into Siauliai airfield this week to patrol the skies over the Baltic countries, three more than normally used since the NATO policing mission was upgraded after the Crimean crisis in 2014. The three Baltic states do not operate their own fighter aircraft and rely entirely on their NATO allies for patrols. “We are reinforcing the air police mission for the period (of Zapad). And we are glad to also have additional land troops here,” Lithuanian Deputy Defense Minister Vytautas Umbrasas said at Siauliai, referring to 600 extra U.S. airborne troops being deployed in the Baltic states during Zapad. “This is very helpful in a situation like this,” he said. Tod Wolters, the top U.S. Air Force commander in Europe, said fighter numbers had been increased due to training opportunities in Lithuania, and pointedly avoided mentioning Russia during the news conference in Siauliai. “The air policing mission will remain as it has been. And the purpose of the air policing mission is to protect the sovereign skies of the three Baltic nations,” said Wolters. And the sheer scale of what is coming? Moscow says almost 13,000 Russian and Belarussian servicemen will take part in Zapad, along with around 70 planes and helicopters and 700 pieces of military hardware including tanks, artillery and rocket systems. That is a staggering show of might!

title: Trump's win throws furious Republican security hawks into turmoil – will they cave?
text: They called him unfit to lead. Now they have to decide whether to work for him. Some Republican foreign policy veterans who came out against Donald Trump during the presidential campaign said on Wednesday they were sticking to their guns after his election victory. But a few others signaled that their objections to serving in his new administration were softening. Trump's stunning upset over Democrat Hillary Clinton has thrown the Republican national security establishment into a painful dilemma, since much of it had publicly distanced itself from its own party's candidate, declaring him unfit to lead. Do they now crawl back into the fold? Career diplomats, intelligence officials and military officers face their own agonizing choice: quit their posts out of concern that a Trump presidency would violate their principles, or stay and try to influence policy from the inside. State Department spokesman Mark Toner tried to calm nerves: “I wouldn't expect a mass exodus.” The bad blood runs deep. About 150 of the Republican party's most prominent national security specialists signed open letters in March and August in outright opposition to Trump's candidacy. One said he was “utterly” unqualified for the White House. The other warned that he would be “the most reckless president in American history.” Neither letter said the former officials would never work for Trump, but their scathing critique was clearly meant to scare fellow Republicans away from supporting him. Trump hit back hard at the time, deriding them as members of “the failed Washington elite” who “deserve the blame for making the world such a dangerous place.” And a number of the signatories contacted on Wednesday made it clear they were unswayed from their negative view of Trump and would not work for him!

title: Bloodbath in Almaty: gunman storms police station, slaughters five
text: A gunman stormed a police station on Monday in Almaty, the largest city in Kazakhstan, and killed three officers and two civilians in a brutal attack attributed to radical Islamist motivations. The bloodshed has sharpened fears about the spread of terrorism in former Soviet Central Asia as an oil bust ripples through regional economies and the Islamic State's footprint expands. Police in Almaty said the attacker wrested a rifle from a guard at a police station, wounded him and then turned the weapon on three police officers, killing them. As the battle raged, the gunman shot dead one of the two civilian victims and then hijacked his Toyota Corolla. He was later caught by the police and taken into custody. The confusion was striking. Early on Monday, officers said two men had attacked the police station. Later they backtracked: the second suspect was in fact a hostage, a taxi driver forced to drive the gunman to the scene of the attack. And the toll kept climbing. Tass, the Russian news agency, reported that more than a dozen other people were wounded, and a local news portal said seven police officers were in intensive care with gunshot wounds. Who was behind it? The authorities alternately described the rampage as the work of criminals on the run after killing a woman over the weekend, or of Islamic radicals, though the two theories are not mutually exclusive. On Monday evening, President Nursultan Nazarbayev called the shooting a terrorist attack. Security officials said the suspect, a resident of western Kazakhstan, had converted to fundamentalist Salafi Islam while serving a prison term for robbery. It is a chilling blow to Kazakhstan, an oil producer with major investments from Chevron and Exxon that has been a bastion of stability for most of the period.

title: Vodka, betrayal and a brutal end: the final hours of Yemen's Saleh
text: A day before they killed Yemen's former president, gunmen from the Iran-aligned Houthi militia group overran one of Ali Abdullah Saleh's fortified compounds in Sanaa. They ransacked the villa, snapped photos of liquor flasks and vodka bottles and posted them online for all to see. “This is how the traitor (Saleh) and his family lived during a time of war, siege and cholera,” Hamid Rizq, a senior Houthi official, said on his official Twitter account. The Houthi gunmen moved fast and without mercy to punish the 75-year-old Saleh for having appeared to switch sides in Yemen's three-year civil war, a proxy battle for influence between regional powers Iran and Saudi Arabia. Saleh had been allied with the Houthis for three years. Then, on Saturday, he called for a new page in relations with Saudi Arabia. Two days later he was dead. The murder is a heavy blow for Riyadh, which had hoped the backing of Saleh and his loyalist army units in northern Yemen would help close a war that has killed 10,000 people and caused one of the world's most acute humanitarian crises. Saudi Arabia fears the Houthis will become as powerful a force in the Middle East as Lebanon's Iran-backed Hezbollah. And the Houthis are not budging. They are holding their ground despite air strikes by Saudi Arabia and its allies and a naval blockade that has kept food, medicine and fuel out of Houthi-controlled northern areas, pushing the region to the brink of famine. Last month, the Houthis fired a ballistic missile into Riyadh. So what now? The Saudis are pinning their hopes on Saleh's son Ahmed Ali and his good ties with Saudi ally United Arab Emirates to do the job his father couldn't.

title: Heartbreak in Chattanooga: a mangled school bus and a city torn apart
text: Jasmine Mateen was standing outside her home on Tuesday afternoon when her cellphone went off. Two of her daughters, hurt when their school bus crashed on Monday, were being discharged from the hospital. For a brief moment the news pulled her out of her grief. Only moments before, Ms. Mateen had been talking about her daughter Zyaira, the girl with the new coat, who died in the very same bus crash that injured two of Ms. Mateen's other daughters. How does a mother bear that? “My baby's coming home, but her sister's dead,” Ms. Mateen said as a single tear rolled down her left cheek. “Even though she was the one who told me my baby was dead, I just didn't want to believe it,” she said of Zasmyn. The third daughter on board, Zacauree'A Brown, is 10. “I couldn't believe it. You know how you try to hold on to hope?” The whole city, just north of Tennessee's border with Georgia, reeled on Tuesday as it faced the grim toll of the deadly crash. The authorities said that at least five Woodmore Elementary School students, four girls and a boy, had died, and that 12 others were still hospitalized. Six of the children were in intensive care. Elsewhere in Chattanooga, the bus driver, Johnthony K. Walker, 24, sat in jail, charged with vehicular homicide after the authorities said he had recklessly sped and swerved during his afternoon route. Reckless! “We are heartbroken for all of our students and their families,” said Kirk Kelly, the interim schools superintendent in Hamilton County. “Yesterday was the worst day that we have had for Woodmore and for Hamilton County Schools that I can recall in my life as an educator and as a parent and as a member of this community.”

title: Far right on the brink of power as Austria's Kurz opens the door!
text: Austria's conservative leader Sebastian Kurz will hold coalition talks with the far-right Freedom Party (FPO), both sides said on Tuesday, pushing the anti-immigration party a dramatic step closer to power, which it last held more than a decade ago. Kurz's party won last week's parliamentary election with 31.5 percent of the vote, but that leaves it far short of a majority. It needs a partner to control parliament and form a stable government, and only two parties have enough seats to do that: the Social Democrats (SPO) and the FPO. And the choice? Hardly a surprise. Kurz, 31, took a hard line on immigration in the campaign that left little daylight between him and the FPO, and both parties exploited a widespread feeling that the country had been overrun during Europe's migration crisis in 2015 and 2016. When he took over as leader of the People's Party (OVP) in May, he demanded an end to the current coalition with the SPO, arguing for a break with Austria's tradition of often deadlocked centrist coalitions. That left the FPO, a party founded by former Nazis in the 1950s, as the more willing partner. Founded by former Nazis! “I have therefore decided to invite (FPO leader) Heinz-Christian Strache and the FPO today to take part in coalition talks,” Kurz told a news conference. Strache wasted no time accepting, saying teams from both parties would meet on Wednesday, but warning that the FPO would not strike a deal at any cost. “Being part of the government is not an end in itself and only makes sense if we can implement our correct and important policies,” Strache told a news conference. “Therefore no one should think that we will make it easy for the OVP.”

title: NATO sounds the alarm: is Russia building a banned nuclear-capable missile?
text: NATO allies on Friday publicly raised the alarm over a Russian cruise missile system that the alliance says may break a Cold War-era pact banning such weapons, rallying behind Washington. The stakes could hardly be higher. The United States believes Russia is developing a ground-launched cruise missile system with a range that is prohibited by a 1987 treaty, one that could give Russia the ability to launch a nuclear strike on Europe on short notice. A nuclear strike on short notice! “Allies have identified a Russian missile system that raises serious concerns,” the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation said in a statement. “NATO urges Russia to address these concerns in a substantial and transparent way, and actively engage in a technical dialogue with the United States.” In a separate statement, the U.S. envoy to NATO, Kay Bailey Hutchison, said: “Russia's behavior raises serious concerns.” Russia has denied it is violating the 1987 Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty. Of course it has. U.S.-led NATO's concerns are likely to strain relations between Moscow and the West even further, and they are already at a low over Russia's 2014 seizure of Crimea, Western sanctions on the Russian economy and U.S. accusations that Moscow used computer hackers to influence the 2016 U.S. presidential election. Moscow denies that it interfered in the election. The NATO statement follows a meeting between Russia and the United States in Geneva this week to mark the 30th anniversary of the treaty between the United States and the Soviet Union. Some celebration. According to an April U.S. State Department report, Washington determined in 2016 that Russia was in violation of its treaty obligations not to possess, produce, or flight-test a ground-launched cruise missile with a range capability of 500 km to 5,500 km (310-3,417 miles), or to possess or produce launchers of such missiles.

title: $18 billion shell game? Lawmakers clash over Pentagon war-funding 'gimmick'
text: Is Congress playing games with the troops' money? U.S. lawmakers in the House Armed Services Committee began debating an annual defense policy bill on Wednesday that would shift a whopping $18 billion in Pentagon war-funding to other military needs. The proposed legislation would use the $18 billion to halt cuts to the size of the military and boost training and maintenance in a push to improve U.S. military readiness. But the funding shift would leave just $35.7 billion to pay for U.S. military efforts in Afghanistan, Iraq and Syria. The House panel insisted that was enough to last through April 2017, giving the next president time to evaluate the security situation and make a supplemental budget request to Congress. Not everyone is buying it. Representative Madeleine Bordallo, a Democrat from Guam, said she was “concerned that the short-sighted budget gimmick ... may leave our troops short of funding required in the near future.” Representative Mac Thornberry, chairman of the committee, shot back that while “some people may call it a gimmick,” the Democratic majority in 2008 had done something very similar. The backdrop is grim. The U.S. military has warned again and again in recent years that ongoing efforts to trim nearly $1 trillion from projected defense budgets over a decade have forced it to postpone training, maintenance and upkeep. The measure, the National Defense Authorization Act, sets U.S. defense policy and authorizes, but does not appropriate, funding for the Pentagon. Lawmakers in the House panel expected to vote on the final version early on Thursday, after which it will go to the full House of Representatives. The draft bill unveiled by Thornberry this week would authorize a massive $610.5 billion in defense spending for the 2017 fiscal year beginning in October, in line with the defense spending plan proposed by Obama earlier this year.

title: Harvey's $180 billion devastation – and Washington is bickering over the bill!
text: Texas is under water, and Washington is arguing about money. Harvey, which slammed ashore on Aug. 25 as the most powerful hurricane to hit Texas in more than 50 years, has killed an estimated 50 people, displaced more than 1 million and damaged some 200,000 homes in a path of destruction stretching more than 300 miles (480 km). As the city of Houston and the region's critical energy infrastructure began to recover nine days after the storm hit, the fight over how to pay for the disaster erupted in Washington. Texas Governor Greg Abbott put the damage at $150 billion to $180 billion, calling it more costly than Hurricanes Katrina or Sandy, which devastated New Orleans in 2005 and New York in 2012. The administration of President Donald Trump has asked Congress for an initial $7.85 billion for recovery efforts, a mere fraction of what will eventually be needed. Republican lawmakers, who control both houses of Congress, have traditionally fought against raising the debt ceiling. But with people suffering and large areas of the fourth-largest U.S. city under water, tying the issue to Harvey aid could force their hand. Will they really stand in the way?

title: Dubai's dazzling new landmark – stolen from the man who designed it?
text: Few cities on earth can rival Dubai for sheer verticality. The pale sands of this once forgettable port beside the emptiness of the Arabian desert have sprouted every kind of skyscraper imaginable. They rise as if conjured by an obsession with Las Vegas and a craving for altitude. The Burj Khalifa, the tallest structure on the planet, soars to twice the height of the Empire State Building. Now Dubai is about to get yet another trophy. The Dubai Frame, set to open this year, is literally and figuratively a frame placed over the overwhelming view: two parallel towers linked by an observation deck. It marks how far the city has come, drawing the eye from the drab buildings of the old settlement along Dubai Creek to the riotous jumble of skyscrapers stretching south to the Persian Gulf. It is a totem of Dubai's ambitions. And it may be a fake. The architect whose original design inspired the structure, Fernando Donis, has accused the Dubai municipality of breaching his copyright in a lawsuit filed in December in United States federal court. Nine years ago, Mr. Donis won an international competition to design the building, beating more than 900 other entrants. Yet he was shut out of the project's execution and never paid for his intellectual property, his lawsuit claims. Shut out and unpaid! “It's shocking,” Mr. Donis said. “The Frame is mine, and they don't want to grant that it is mine. The infringement doesn't just victimize me. They have taken something from all architects — the protection of our ideas.” Raised as a monument to Dubai's dreams of being a hub of international commerce, the Frame now stands as a physical monument to the crude system that built it.

title: Jail staff left paralyzed man on cell floor for five days before his death

He fell to the floor and called for help, telling jail staff that he could not move and that he had broken his neck. For the next ten hours, Williams lay motionless on the floor of the holding cell. He received no medical attention during that time.

title: Your map is wrong! Australia is on the move – and the whole country must relocate
text: That map of Australia you own? It's wrong. And the entire country is going to officially relocate to fix the error. Incredible, but true. The culprit is plate tectonics, the shifting of huge chunks of the earth's surface. Australia sits on one of these pieces, and by geological standards it is practically flying: about 2.7 inches northward a year, with a slight clockwise rotation as well. People on the ground may not notice, but the Global Positioning System certainly does. So Australia has to adjust its longitudes and latitudes to line up with GPS coordinates. Four times in the last 50 years, Australia has reset the official coordinates of everything in the country to make them more accurate, correcting for other sources of error as well as continental drift. The last adjustment, in 1994, was a whopper: about 656 feet, enough to give the delivery driver an alibi for ringing your neighbor's doorbell instead of yours. “You might think, ‘Where's my pizza? ’” said Dan Jaksa of Geoscience Australia, the government agency that worries about the coordinates. But far more is at stake than pizza, he said: intelligent transportation systems that will rely on the sharper accuracy coming with the next generation of GPS technology. The next adjustment, due at the end of the year, will be about 1.5 meters (4.9 feet). That is not really enough to throw off satellite navigation systems, which are generally accurate only to within 15 to 30 feet. But the next generation of GPS devices, using both satellites and ground stations, will be accurate to within an inch or less. And new technologies that depend on pinpoint location will be vital to Australia's future. Who knew a continent could go astray?

title: Wind industry rejoices as Senate rescues vital tax credit – but the fight isn't over!
text: Huge relief for wind power! The U.S. wind energy industry on Friday cheered a Senate tax proposal that, unlike the House version unveiled last week, preserves the tax credit that helps wind farms compete with plants fired by fossil fuels. The industry had spent a frantic week warning lawmakers on Capitol Hill that changes to the credit would put $50 billion in planned investment at risk. But can it celebrate yet? Not quite. If the House and Senate pass their differing versions of the Republicans' sweeping tax-cut plan, a House-Senate committee will have to reconcile the differences and both chambers will have to approve the resulting compromise, so it is too soon to know whether the tax overhaul will ultimately save the wind energy credit. The stakes are enormous. MidAmerican Energy said on Thursday that if the bill passed as the House proposed, the Berkshire Hathaway Inc unit could be forced to scrap $4.3 billion of wind investments in Iowa, hitting 400 jobs and wiping out $10 million a year in property tax and landowner payments. The wind industry's production tax credit was extended by Congress in 2015 and awards a credit for every kilowatt-hour of energy produced from wind projects. Investors and project developers had banked on the stability of the policy, which is scheduled to phase out by 2020, when planning their investments. “The Senate tax reform bill keeps a promise to America's more than 100,000 wind energy workers and restores the confidence of businesses pouring billions of dollars into rural America,” Tom Kiernan, Chief Executive of the American Wind Energy Association trade group, said in a statement. Republican Senators Chuck Grassley of Iowa, John Thune of South Dakota and Dean Heller of Nevada and others had opposed changes to the tax credit, the AWEA said.

title: Junk-rated Chicago gambles on a bold new debt scheme to stop the bleeding
text: Can Chicago dig itself out of its debt hole? Under a plan announced on Wednesday by the mayor's office, the cash-strapped city would create a new entity to issue bonds backed by its share of Illinois sales tax collections, in a bid to cut its borrowing costs. Mayor Rahm Emanuel unveiled the plan at the city's annual investors conference, promising it will be “much more financially viable” for Chicago. The city badly needs it. A chronic structural budget deficit and a gigantic unfunded pension liability that totaled $35.76 billion at the end of 2016 have dragged the city's general obligation (GO) credit ratings from the low end of investment grade all the way down to junk. Junk! As a result, investors have demanded higher interest rates for the city's debt. Illinois' fiscal 2018 budget, enacted last month, included a provision allowing home-rule local governments like Chicago to assign their state revenue to an entity for the purpose of issuing debt. Carole Brown, Chicago's chief financial officer, said the state sales tax dollars would flow first through the new entity to meet debt service and other requirements before any of the revenue is released to the city's general fund. The state law also creates a statutory lien that would shield the bonds from a bankruptcy filing, which Illinois local governments are currently not allowed to pursue. “It's one of the reasons that we expect the market will view (the new debt) favorably, why it will get higher ratings and why we think the cost differential with our (GO bonds) will be so great,” Brown said. An ordinance creating the program will be introduced in the city council this fall, according to Brown. If it passes, Chicago would first refund some of its “more expensive” GO debt and outstanding sales tax revenue bonds, she said, pointing out that New York, Philadelphia and Washington have similarly structured debt programs.

title: Exclusive: Justice Department quietly guts protections for immigrant children in court
text: The U.S. Justice Department has quietly issued new guidelines for immigration judges that strip out some instructions on how to protect unaccompanied juveniles appearing in their courtrooms. A Dec. 20 memo, issued by the Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR), replaces 2007 guidelines that spelled out policies and procedures judges should follow when dealing with children who crossed the border illegally alone and face possible deportation. And what is gone? The new memo scraps suggestions from the 2007 memo on how to conduct “child-sensitive questioning” and adds reminders to judges to maintain “impartiality” even though “juvenile cases may present sympathetic allegations.” Even the word “child” is replaced with “unmarried individual under the age of 18” in many instances. Cold, clinical language for frightened kids. An EOIR official insisted the new memo contained “clarifications and updates” to 10-year-old guidance “in order to be consistent with the laws as they've been passed by Congress.” The new memo was posted on the Justice Department website but has not been previously reported. Immigration advocates fear the new guidelines could make court appearances for children even harder, and a spokeswoman for the union representing immigration judges said judges are concerned about the tone of the memo. President Donald Trump has made tougher immigration enforcement a key policy goal of his administration, and has zeroed in on trying to curb the illegal entry of children. The administration says it wants to stop vulnerable juveniles from making perilous journeys to the United States and to root out fraud from programs for young immigrants. One rewritten section of the memo focuses on how to make children comfortable in the court ahead of hearings.

title: Shamed and ignored: why obese patients get worse care from doctors who can't see past the fat
text: “You must lose weight,” a doctor told Sarah Bramblette, advising a diet. But Ms. Bramblette had a simple question: How much do I weigh? The doctor's scale only went up to 350 pounds, and she was heavier than that. If she did not know the number, how would she know whether the diet was working? The doctor had no answer. None! So Ms. Bramblette, 39, who lived in Ohio at the time, was forced into a solution that made her burn with shame. She drove to a nearby junkyard that had a scale big enough to weigh her. She was 502 pounds. A junkyard! One in three Americans is obese, a rate that has been climbing steadily for more than two decades, yet the health care system, in its attitudes, equipment and common practices, is shockingly ill prepared, and its practitioners are often unwilling, to treat the growing population of fat patients. The failures run from scales and scanners, like M.R.I. machines that are not built big enough for very heavy people, to surgeons who flatly refuse to give knee or hip replacements to the obese, to drug doses that have never been calibrated for obese patients. It is especially grim for the more than 15 million Americans who have extreme obesity, a body mass index of 40 or higher, and face a wide range of health concerns. Part of the problem, both patients and doctors say, is a refusal to look beyond a fat person's weight. Patty Nece, 58, of Alexandria, Va., went to an orthopedist because her hip was aching. She had lost nearly 70 pounds and, although she still had a way to go, was feeling good about herself. Then she saw the doctor.
